fig11_1: Semilog convergence plot for differentiating e to the power sine x on a periodic grid: the horizontal axis is the number of grid points N (linear) and the vertical axis is the maximum error (logarithmic). Two overlapping curves, one for the dense circulant matrix and one for the FFT route, fall exponentially with N and flatten near ten to the power minus fifteen for N at or above thirty, showing the two methods are numerically identical and both reach machine precision.
fig11_2: Log-log timing plot with the grid size N on the horizontal axis and wall-clock time on the vertical axis. The dense matrix curve rises as a steep straight line of slope two (order N squared), while the FFT curve rises much more gently (order N log N); the widening vertical gap shows the FFT becoming about a thousand times faster by N equal to two thousand forty-eight.
fig11_3: Two-panel comparison of linear advection after one full period at N equal to one hundred twenty-eight. Left panel plots the solution profile versus x: the blue Fourier spectral curve sits exactly on the exact Gaussian pulse, while the red dashed second-order upwind finite-difference curve is broadened and lagged by numerical dispersion and dissipation. Right panel shows pointwise error versus x on a logarithmic scale: the spectral error hovers near machine precision while the finite-difference error is many orders of magnitude larger.
fig11_4: Two-panel evolution of the viscous Burgers equation with viscosity zero point zero one starting from sine x. Left panel is a space-time color map (x horizontal, time vertical) where the smooth sine wave steepens into a sharp near-vertical front around x equal to pi. Right panel overlays solution profiles versus x at several increasing times, showing the sine progressively sharpening into a thin viscous shock layer.
fig11_5: Two-panel study of dealiasing for Burgers at time one. Left panel plots the energy spectrum, magnitude of u-hat-k squared, versus wavenumber on a logarithmic vertical scale for runs with and without the two-thirds rule; the undealiased curve turns upward and piles energy near the Nyquist wavenumber, while the dealiased curve keeps decaying smoothly. Right panel shows the two physical-space solutions versus x nearly coinciding, the visible differences being small at this time.
fig11_6: Two-panel Zabusky-Kruskal KdV experiment from initial condition cosine of pi x on the interval zero to two. Left panel is a space-time color map (x horizontal, time vertical) in which the steepening cosine breaks into several diagonal streaks of differing slope, the trajectories of solitons of different amplitudes and speeds. Right panel overlays solution profiles versus x at selected times, showing the smooth cosine splitting into a train of distinct sharp soliton pulses.
fig11_7: Four-panel sequence of a two-soliton KdV collision on the domain zero to eighty, with soliton parameters one and zero point five. Each panel plots the solution versus x at a successive time: before the interaction the taller, faster pulse trails the shorter, slower one; during the collision they merge into a single hump; and afterward both pulses re-emerge with their original shapes intact, only shifted in position relative to where they would have been without interaction.
fig11_8: Two-panel nonlinear Schrödinger simulation from the perturbed plane wave one plus zero point one cosine x. Left panel is a space-time color map of the amplitude magnitude of u (x horizontal, time vertical) showing repeating bands of focused modulation, the recurrence cycles driven by modulation instability. Right panel plots the relative deviation of the L-two norm from its initial value versus time, staying flat at the level of machine precision and confirming the split-step method conserves the norm.
fig11_9: Space-time color map of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation on a domain of length thirty-two pi, with x on the horizontal axis and time on the vertical axis. After a brief transient the field settles into a statistically steady pattern of cellular stripes that continually merge and split, the characteristic fingerprint of spatiotemporal chaos handled stably despite the strong fourth-derivative stiffness.
fig11_10: Time-averaged energy spectrum of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation in its chaotic steady state, plotting energy versus wavenumber on a logarithmic scale. Energy peaks at low wavenumbers within the linearly unstable band where the magnitude of k is below one, then falls off steeply toward high wavenumbers as the fourth-derivative term damps small scales.
fig11_11: Four vorticity snapshots of two-dimensional decaying turbulence on the periodic square zero to two pi, with viscosity ten to the power minus three and N equal to one hundred twenty-eight, shown at times zero, five, ten, and twenty. Each is a color map of vorticity over the plane; the initially fine-grained field of many small positive and negative vortices progressively merges into a few large coherent vortex blobs, illustrating the inverse energy cascade.
fig11_12: Two-panel diagnostics for two-dimensional decaying turbulence, both plotting a quantity versus time. Left panel shows kinetic energy declining slowly and gradually as energy moves to large scales. Right panel shows enstrophy, the mean squared vorticity, decaying much more steeply and rapidly, consistent with the selective decay principle in which enstrophy is dissipated far faster than energy.
fig11_13: Two-panel solution of variable-coefficient transport with wave speed zero point three plus sine squared of x minus one. Left panel is a space-time color map (x horizontal, time vertical) tracing a Gaussian pulse along a curved characteristic that bends as the pulse speeds up in fast regions and slows in slow regions. Right panel is a waterfall view stacking the pulse profiles with vertical offset growing in proportion to time, showing the pulse keeping its shape while translating at variable speed.
fig11_14: Two-panel Schrödinger simulation of a Gaussian wavepacket in a harmonic potential solved by Strang splitting. Left panel is a space-time color map of the probability density, magnitude of u squared (x horizontal, time vertical), tracing a periodic back-and-forth oscillation of the packet within the trap. Right panel is a waterfall plot stacking the probability density profiles at selected times, showing the packet breathing and shifting as it oscillates.
fig11_15: Two-panel Allen-Cahn simulation with epsilon equal to zero point zero five solved by an implicit-explicit scheme. Left panel is a space-time color map (x horizontal, time vertical) in which a small initial perturbation rapidly separates into broad regions near plus one and minus one divided by thin fronts that slowly merge and disappear over time (coarsening). Right panel overlays profiles versus x at selected times, from the noisy initial state through sharp two-phase plateaus to fewer, wider domains.
tbl11_1: Summary table listing the ten computational études of the chapter, giving for each its number, governing PDE, key spectral technique (such as FFT differentiation, two-thirds dealiasing, integrating factor, split-step Fourier, or IMEX), and the matching time stepper (RK4, IF-RK4, Strang, or Euler).
